title: How do you handle a hot row that many requests update at once (e.g. a shared like/stock counter): counter sharding (split into N sub-counters and sum) or buffering increments in Redis and periodically syncing to the DB?
shortTitle: How do you handle a hot row that many requests update at once
keyPoints: A hot row serializes all writers on one row lock, collapsing throughput even though the rest of the system is idle.
Counter sharding splits one logical counter into N physical sub-rows that writers spread across; read is SUM of all shards.
Buffering accumulates increments in Redis with atomic INCR and flushes the aggregate to the DB periodically.
Sharding keeps every increment durable in the DB; buffering trades staleness for extreme throughput.
For real money, avoid a hot counter entirely: model as append-only ledger entries and compute the balance as a sum.
The two techniques compose: sharded Redis counters flushed to the database.
Keep each transaction tiny so the row lock is held briefly, reducing contention even without sharding.

s1_definition.oneliner: A hot row serializes writers on one lock, so either shard the counter into N sub-rows that writers spread across and sum on read, or buffer increments in Redis and flush the aggregate to the DB periodically.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Hot row** – A single database row that many concurrent requests try to update, creating lock contention that serializes all writers.
- **Counter sharding** – Split one logical counter into N physical sub-counter rows; writers spread across them, readers SUM all N.
- **Buffering** – Accumulate increments in a fast store (Redis INCR) and periodically flush the aggregate to the database.
- **Append-only ledger** – For real money, model each change as an appended entry and compute the balance, avoiding the hot row entirely.
- **Trade-offs** – Sharding keeps increments durable; buffering trades staleness for throughput.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a single donation box at National Bank of India where thousands of customers must drop coins one at a time, so everyone queues. Counter sharding puts out twenty donation boxes so twenty people donate at once, and at the end you add up all twenty. Buffering lets a fast assistant collect everyone's coins in a bucket and tip the whole bucket into the main box once a minute.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A hot row serializes all writers on one row-level lock, collapsing throughput even though the database has plenty of CPU. The two main remedies are counter sharding, which splits one counter into N sub-rows so writers spread across N locks and the true value is their SUM, and Redis buffering, which accumulates increments with atomic INCR and flushes the aggregate periodically.

Sharding keeps every increment durable in the database and is the right choice when the source of truth must stay there. Buffering trades staleness for extreme throughput and suits approximate counters like likes or views. The two compose: sharded Redis counters flushed to the database.

The most important lesson for banking is that for real money, you should not use a hot shared counter at all. At National Bank of India, Pankaj models each balance change as an append-only ledger entry and computes the balance as a SUM, which removes the hot row by design while maintaining full ACID guarantees and an audit trail.

Remember one sentence: a hot row serializes on one lock, so either shard the counter into N sub-rows, buffer in Redis and flush periodically, or for real money avoid the hot row entirely with an append-only ledger aggregate.
